phy_ocra.5.0.summary: To **stretch, bend or compress** an object you must apply **more than one force**: a single force would just make the whole object accelerate rather than change its shape. A change of shape is called a **deformation**. If the object returns to its original shape and size when the forces are removed the deformation is **elastic**; if it stays permanently changed it is **plastic** (inelastic). OCR expects you to explain why more than one force is needed and to describe and give examples of both types of deformation caused by stretching forces.

core.p: Deformation is any **change in the shape or size** of an object caused by forces. The three main ways an object can be deformed are **stretching** (tension), **compressing** (squashing) and **bending**. Deformation happens because the forces push or pull different parts of the object in different directions, so the particles in the material move relative to each other.
bullets: Stretching: pulling forces act outwards on opposite ends, so the object gets longer.
Compressing: pushing forces act inwards on opposite ends, so the object gets shorter.
Bending: forces act at different points so one side is stretched and the other compressed.
Twisting is another kind of deformation, but OCR focuses on stretching, compressing and bending.

callouts.p: A change in the shape or size of an object caused by forces acting on it.

core.h: Why more than one force is needed
core.p: If only **one force** acts on an object, there is a **resultant force**, so by Newton's second law the whole object simply **accelerates** in the direction of that force; it does not change shape. To change shape, the object must be held in place by at least one other force so that different parts are pulled or pushed in different directions.
bullets: One force alone: the object moves (accelerates) as a whole.
Two (or more) forces: the object can stay still while being deformed.
For a stretched spring, the hook pulls up and the weight pulls down.
For a squashed ball, your hand pushes down and the table pushes up.
For a bent ruler, forces act at both ends and in the middle.

callouts.p: To stretch, bend or compress an object, more than one force has to be applied.
Explain with Newton's second law: one unbalanced force would make the object accelerate instead of deforming.

core.p: An object is **elastically deformed** if it **returns to its original shape and size** when the deforming forces are removed. The particles are pulled slightly apart (or pushed closer) but the bonds between them are not broken or rearranged, so they spring back.
bullets: Returns completely to original length and shape.
Energy stored in the **elastic potential energy store** can be fully recovered.
Examples: a spring with a small load, a rubber band, a bouncing ball, a trampoline.
Happens for small forces, below the elastic limit.

callouts.p: A deformation in which the object returns to its original shape and size when the forces are removed.

core.p: An object is **plastically deformed** if it **does not return to its original shape** when the forces are removed: it is **permanently** changed. The layers of particles have slid past each other into new positions, so there is nothing to pull them back.
bullets: Permanent change of shape or length.
Not all the energy transferred is stored elastically; some is dissipated (mainly heating).
Examples: modelling clay, a crushed drinks can, a car body in a crash, a spring stretched too far, chewing gum.
Usually happens when forces are large enough to exceed the elastic limit.

callouts.p: A deformation in which the object does not return to its original shape when the forces are removed; the change is permanent.
Plastic deformation has nothing to do with the material plastic. Many plastics deform elastically and many metals deform plastically.

core.p: The key test is simple: **remove the force and look**. If the object goes back to exactly its original shape it was elastic; if it is still bent, longer or squashed, it was plastic.
bullets: Elastic: temporary, reversible.
Plastic: permanent, irreversible.
The same object can show both: elastic for small forces, plastic for large forces.

core.p: Many materials behave elastically for small forces but plastically once the force passes a certain point, called the **elastic limit**. Beyond it the object will not return to its original length. A spring stretched too far stays slightly longer and looks uncoiled.
bullets: Below the elastic limit: elastic deformation.
Above the elastic limit: plastic (permanent) deformation.
A spring loaded past its elastic limit has a permanent extension when unloaded.
The linear (proportional) part of force-extension graphs is covered in P2.3c-f.

callouts.p: The maximum force (or extension) an object can take and still return to its original shape when the force is removed.

core.p: For stretching, the two forces act **away from each other** along the same line. In a hanging spring, the support pulls upwards and the weight of the load pulls downwards. The forces are equal in size when the spring is stationary, so the resultant force is zero but the spring is still stretched.
bullets: Stretching forces are also called tensile forces.
Equal and opposite forces on a stationary spring: no acceleration, but deformation.
The larger the stretching forces, the larger the extension.
Extension = new length - original length.

callouts.p: Extension is measured from the original length, not the total length of the spring.

core.p: In compression the two forces push **towards** each other, squashing the object. In bending, forces at different points make the object curve: the outside of the bend is stretched and the inside is compressed at the same time.
bullets: Compression examples: car suspension springs, a sponge, shoe soles.
Bending examples: a diving board, a shelf under books, a fishing rod.
A bent ruler that springs back has deformed elastically.
A bent paperclip that stays bent has deformed plastically.

core.p: Work is done when forces deform an object. For **elastic** deformation this energy is stored in the **elastic potential energy store** and can be transferred back, as when a stretched catapult launches a stone. For **plastic** deformation some of the work done is dissipated, usually as heating of the material, and cannot be recovered.
bullets: Elastic: energy stored, then released when force removed.
Plastic: energy goes into rearranging particles and heating.
Car crumple zones deform plastically to absorb energy in a crash.
Calculating energy stored in a spring is covered in P2.3c-f.

callouts.p: Crumple zones use plastic deformation on purpose so the energy is not returned to the passengers.

core.p: Engineers choose materials depending on whether they need elastic or plastic behaviour. Good exam answers link the type of deformation to the purpose.
bullets: Springs in mattresses and car suspension: must stay elastic.
Bungee cords: elastic, so they return energy and pull the jumper back.
Crumple zones and crash helmets: designed to deform plastically or crush.
Pressing car body panels from sheet steel: uses plastic deformation to shape metal.
Climbing ropes: stretch elastically to reduce the force in a fall.

core.p: A simple practical: hang a spring or rubber band from a clamp, add masses one at a time, then remove them and measure the length each time. If the length returns to the original value, the deformation so far was elastic. If not, the elastic limit has been passed.
bullets: Measure the original length with a ruler at eye level to avoid parallax.
Add masses in equal steps and record the length.
Remove the load and check whether the original length is restored.
Wear eye protection in case a band snaps; keep feet clear of falling masses.

callouts.p: Stretched springs and rubber bands store energy and can snap back; wear safety goggles.

analogy.t: A crowd holding hands versus a crowd that lets go
analogy.p: Picture a line of people holding hands. Pull the ends gently and the line stretches, but everyone still holds hands, so when you let go they spring back to their places: elastic deformation. Pull too hard and people let go and grab new partners further along; when you stop pulling they stay in their new positions: plastic deformation. The people are particles and the handholds are the forces between them. Where it breaks down: real particles do not choose to let go, and in a metal layers of particles slide past each other rather than individual bonds being chosen.

Deformation where the object returns to its original shape when the forces are removed.
Deformation where the object does not return to its original shape; the change is permanent.
Another name for plastic deformation.
The point beyond which an object no longer returns to its original shape when the force is removed.
Deforming an object by pulling it with forces acting away from each other.
Deforming an object by pushing it with forces acting towards each other.
Deformation where forces at different points make an object curve.
The increase in length of an object when it is stretched: new length minus original length.
The length of an object with no deforming forces acting on it.
The single force with the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
The energy store of a stretched, compressed or bent elastic object.
A pulling force that tends to stretch an object.
A change of shape that remains after the forces are removed.

mistakes.w: You only need one force to stretch a spring.
mistakes.r: More than one force is needed; one force alone would make the spring accelerate.

mistakes.w: Plastic deformation is when a plastic object changes shape.
mistakes.r: Plastic deformation means a permanent change of shape, in any material.

mistakes.w: Elastic means it stretches a lot.
mistakes.r: Elastic means it returns to its original shape when the force is removed.

mistakes.w: Extension is the total length of the spring.
mistakes.r: Extension = new length minus original length.

mistakes.w: Plastic deformation happens below the elastic limit.
mistakes.r: Plastic deformation happens when the elastic limit is exceeded.

mistakes.w: A spring that has been stretched always goes back to the same length.
mistakes.r: Only if it was not stretched beyond its elastic limit.

mistakes.w: The forces on a stationary stretched spring are unbalanced.
mistakes.r: They are balanced (resultant zero), yet the spring is still deformed.

mistakes.w: All the energy used in plastic deformation is stored.
mistakes.r: Some is dissipated, mainly by heating; it cannot all be recovered.

exam.q: State what is meant by elastic deformation.
model: The object returns to its original shape (and size) when the forces are removed.
exam.tip: Must include when the force is removed.

exam.q: State what is meant by plastic deformation.
model: The object does not return to its original shape when the forces are removed / permanent change of shape.
exam.tip: Use the word permanent.

exam.q: Explain why more than one force is needed to stretch a spring.
model: With only one force there would be a resultant force.
So the spring would accelerate (move) rather than stretch.
exam.tip: Link to Newton's second law.

exam.q: Give one example of an object that deforms elastically and one that deforms plastically.
model: Elastic: e.g. rubber band / spring with a small load / trampoline.
Plastic: e.g. modelling clay / crushed can / car body in a crash.
exam.tip: Choose clear everyday examples.

exam.q: Name the three ways an object can be deformed by forces.
model: Stretching and compressing (1 mark).
Bending (1 mark).
exam.tip: All three for full marks.

exam.q: A student hangs a 200 g mass on a spring then removes it. The spring returns to 5.0 cm. The original length was 5.0 cm. What type of deformation occurred? Explain.
model: Elastic deformation.
Because the spring returned to its original length when the force was removed.
exam.tip: Always justify using the data.

exam.q: Describe how a student could test whether a rubber band deforms elastically when loaded with 300 g.
model: Measure the original length of the band with a ruler.
Hang the 300 g mass from the band (from a clamp stand).
Remove the mass and measure the length again.
If the length equals the original length, deformation was elastic; if longer, plastic.
exam.tip: Include measuring before and after.

exam.q: Explain why car crumple zones are designed to deform plastically.
model: Plastic deformation absorbs energy (work done on the crumple zone).
The energy is not returned to the car/passengers, so less harm.
exam.tip: Contrast with elastic, which would give energy back.

exam.q: A spring is loaded past its elastic limit. Describe what you would observe when the load is removed.
model: The spring does not return to its original length.
It is permanently longer / coils stay stretched.
exam.tip: Say permanently.

exam.q: Compare elastic and plastic deformation, referring to forces, shape, energy and examples.
model: Both need more than one force acting to stretch, compress or bend the object.
Elastic: the object returns to its original shape when the forces are removed.
Plastic: the object is permanently deformed and does not return.
Elastic deformation happens below the elastic limit; plastic when it is exceeded.
Elastic: energy stored in the elastic store can be recovered; plastic: some energy is dissipated.
Examples: spring/rubber band (elastic); clay/crushed can (plastic).
exam.tip: Structure as similarities then differences.

worked.q: A spring has an original length of 4.0 cm. With a load its length is 6.5 cm. When the load is removed it is 4.3 cm. Calculate the extension when loaded and state the type of deformation.
steps: After unloading the length is 4.3 cm, not 4.0 cm.
So there is a permanent extension of 4.3 - 4.0 = 0.3 cm.
The spring did not return to its original length, so the elastic limit was exceeded.
worked.ans: Extension 2.5 cm; the deformation was plastic (permanent extension 0.3 cm).

worked.q: Explain, in terms of forces, how a person bends a ruler and what type of deformation occurs if it springs back flat.
steps: The person holds both ends and pushes the middle (or pushes one end down while the other is clamped).
So more than one force acts on the ruler, at different points.
The resultant force is zero, so the ruler does not move off, but it bends.
The outside of the curve is stretched and the inside compressed.
When released it returns to flat, its original shape.
worked.ans: More than one force acting at different points bends the ruler; it springs back, so the deformation is elastic.

phy_ocra.5.1.summary: For a spring stretched within its **limit of proportionality**, the extension is **directly proportional** to the force applied, so its force-extension graph is a **straight line through the origin** (a linear relationship) obeying **force = spring constant x extension (F = kx)**. Beyond that limit the graph curves (non-linear). The work done in stretching is stored in the **elastic potential energy store** and equals the **area under the force-extension graph**, which for a linear spring is **energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2**. You must be able to calculate both, convert units, and describe the practical used to investigate force and extension.

core.p: When you stretch a spring with a force, its length increases. The **extension** is the increase in length compared with its **original (unstretched) length**. The bigger the stretching force, the bigger the extension, but exactly how they are related depends on the material and on how far it is stretched.
bullets: Extension = stretched length - original length.
Always measure extension from the original length, not from zero on the ruler.
Force is measured in newtons (N); extension in metres (m) for calculations.
The stretching force from a hanging mass equals its weight: W = m x g, with g = 10 N/kg.

callouts.p: The increase in length of an object when a force stretches it: extension = new length - original length.

core.p: A **linear** relationship gives a **straight-line graph**. If the line also passes through the origin, the two quantities are **directly proportional**: doubling the force doubles the extension. A **non-linear** relationship gives a **curved graph**, where equal increases in force do not give equal increases in extension.
bullets: Spring within limit of proportionality: linear, directly proportional.
Spring beyond limit of proportionality: non-linear, graph curves.
Rubber band: non-linear for most of its stretch.
Polythene strip: non-linear, stretches a lot for little extra force once it starts to yield.

callouts.p: Extension is directly proportional to force only up to the limit of proportionality.

core.p: The **limit of proportionality** is the point on the force-extension graph where the straight line starts to curve. Up to this point F = kx works. Beyond it, extension increases more for each newton added and the spring may also pass its **elastic limit** and be permanently stretched.
bullets: Up to limit of proportionality: straight-line graph.
Beyond it: graph curves, F = kx no longer applies.
The elastic limit is usually at or just beyond the limit of proportionality.
Past the elastic limit the spring does not return to its original length.

callouts.p: The point beyond which force and extension are no longer directly proportional.
The limit of proportionality and the elastic limit are not the same thing, although they are often close together.

core.p: Within the limit of proportionality, the force needed to stretch a spring is **directly proportional** to its extension. The constant of proportionality is the **spring constant, k**. This is often called Hooke's law.
bullets: force (N) = spring constant (N/m) x extension (m).
F = k x x.
Rearranged: k = F / x and x = F / k.
The same equation applies to compressing a spring, where x is the compression.

callouts.p: force = spring constant x extension (F = kx)

core.p: The spring constant tells you how **stiff** a spring is: it is the force needed per metre of extension. A **large k** means a stiff spring that needs a big force to stretch it a little. A **small k** means a soft spring that stretches easily.
bullets: k = force / extension.
Higher k: stiffer spring, steeper force-extension graph.
On a force (y) vs extension (x) graph, gradient = k.
On an extension (y) vs force (x) graph, gradient = 1 / k.
Unit N/m; if extension is in cm, convert to m first (divide by 100).

callouts.p: The force needed per unit extension of a spring, measured in N/m; a measure of its stiffness.
Check which axis is which before you use the gradient to find k.

core.p: To stretch a spring a force must move through a distance, so **work is done**. If the spring is not stretched past its elastic limit, the work done is stored as energy in the spring's **elastic potential energy store**, and can be released when the spring is let go.
bullets: Work done = energy transferred.
Elastic deformation: all the work done is stored (and can be recovered).
Beyond the elastic limit, some energy is dissipated by heating the material.
The average force during stretching is half the final force (for a linear spring), which is why the 0.5 appears.

callouts.p: energy transferred in stretching = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2, E = 0.5 k x^2

core.p: This equation gives the energy stored in a spring stretched within its limit of proportionality. Because extension is **squared**, doubling the extension makes the stored energy **four times** bigger.
bullets: E in joules (J), k in N/m, x in m.
Square the extension first, then multiply by k and 0.5.
To find x: x = square root of (2E / k).
To find k: k = 2E / x^2.
Only valid in the linear (proportional) region.

callouts.p: Forgetting to square the extension, or squaring 0.5 x k x x all together. Only x is squared.

core.h: Work done as area under the graph
core.p: The work done in stretching equals the **area under the force-extension graph**. For the linear region the area is a triangle: 0.5 x base x height = 0.5 x x x F = 0.5 x x x kx = 0.5 k x^2. For a non-linear graph you estimate the area by counting squares.
bullets: Area of triangle = 0.5 x extension x force.
This gives the same answer as 0.5 k x^2.
Non-linear graph: count squares under the curve, multiply by the energy per square.
Make sure force is in N and extension in m so area is in J.

callouts.p: If you are given a graph and asked for energy, the area method is usually expected; show your triangle working.

core.h: Required practical: investigating force and extension (PAG P2)
core.p: This practical measures how the extension of a spring depends on the force applied, so you can plot a graph and find the spring constant.
bullets: Clamp a spring to a stand; fix a metre rule vertically beside it with a G-clamp for stability.
Attach a pointer to the bottom of the spring and record the original length.
Add masses in equal steps (e.g. 100 g = 1 N each) and record the new length each time.
Calculate extension = new length - original length.
Plot force (y) against extension (x); draw a line of best fit.
Gradient of the straight part = spring constant k.
Remove masses at the end to check whether the spring returns to its original length (elastic).

callouts.p: Wear eye protection in case the spring snaps; place a tray or cushion below the masses and keep feet clear.

core.p: Good experimental technique reduces errors and gives a reliable spring constant.
bullets: Read the ruler at **eye level** to avoid parallax error.
Use a fixed pointer on the spring so you read the same point each time.
Wait for the spring to stop bouncing before reading.
Repeat readings (loading and unloading) and calculate a mean.
Use small, equal increments of mass to locate the limit of proportionality accurately.
Do not overload: stop once the spring stays permanently stretched.

core.h: Springs in series and other materials
core.p: Grade 9 answers can apply the idea to unfamiliar situations. Different materials show different force-extension curves. A rubber band stores energy but its graph is curved, so F = kx cannot be used and the area must be estimated.
bullets: Rubber band: non-linear curve; extension increases quickly then stiffens.
Metal wire: linear at first, then curves as it yields.
Two identical springs end to end: same force gives double extension, so effective k is halved.
Two identical springs side by side: each takes half the force, so effective k is doubled.

analogy.t: A spring as a savings jar for energy
analogy.p: Stretching a spring is like putting coins in a jar: every bit of work you do pulling it is saved in the elastic store, and you get it all back when you let go, as long as you do not break the jar. The spring constant is how heavy each coin feels: a stiff spring makes every centimetre cost more effort. Going past the elastic limit is like cracking the jar: some coins fall out (energy dissipated) and the jar never closes properly again. Where it breaks down: in a real jar each coin costs the same, but in a spring each extra centimetre costs more force than the last, which is why energy goes with x squared.

A relationship that gives a curved graph.
Two quantities where doubling one doubles the other; straight line through the origin.
The point beyond which force and extension are no longer directly proportional.
The point beyond which a material will not return to its original shape when the force is removed.

mistakes.r: Extension = new length minus original length.

mistakes.w: Leaves extension in cm when calculating k in N/m.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres first (divide by 100).

mistakes.r: E = 0.5 x k x x^2; the extension is squared.

mistakes.r: F = kx only applies up to the limit of proportionality.

mistakes.w: The limit of proportionality is where the spring breaks.
mistakes.r: It is where the graph stops being a straight line.

mistakes.w: Stiffer spring has a smaller spring constant.
mistakes.r: A stiffer spring has a larger spring constant.

mistakes.w: Uses mass in kg as the force.

mistakes.w: Reads the ruler from above or below.
mistakes.r: Read at eye level to avoid parallax error.

exam.q: State the equation linking force, spring constant and extension.
model: force = spring constant x extension (F = kx).
exam.tip: Learn it in words as well as symbols.

exam.q: A spring has original length 12 cm and length 15 cm when loaded. Calculate the extension in metres.
model: Extension = 15 - 12 = 3 cm.
exam.tip: Convert at the end.

exam.q: Describe the difference between a linear and non-linear force-extension relationship.
model: Linear: straight-line graph / extension directly proportional to force.
Non-linear: curved graph / extension not proportional to force.
exam.tip: Mention graph shape.

exam.q: A force of 6.0 N stretches a spring by 0.040 m. Calculate the spring constant.
exam.tip: Include the unit.

exam.q: A spring with k = 200 N/m is stretched by 0.05 m. Calculate the energy stored.
exam.tip: Square the extension first.

exam.q: Explain how a force-extension graph can be used to find the work done in stretching a spring.
model: Work done = area under the force-extension graph.
For the straight-line region, area = 0.5 x force x extension.
exam.tip: Use the triangle area.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by the limit of proportionality and how you would identify it on a graph.
model: The point beyond which force and extension are no longer directly proportional.
Where the straight line on the graph starts to curve.
exam.tip: Two separate ideas: meaning and graph feature.

exam.q: A spring of k = 40 N/m stores 0.80 J. Calculate its extension.
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting if you prefer.

exam.q: The extension of a spring is doubled within its limit of proportionality. State what happens to the force and to the energy stored.
model: Force doubles.
Energy stored increases by a factor of four.
exam.tip: Energy depends on x squared.

exam.q: Describe a method to determine the spring constant of a spring. Include how to make the results accurate.
model: Hang spring from a clamp stand with a vertical metre rule alongside; measure original length using a pointer.
Add masses in equal steps (e.g. 100 g) and measure the new length each time.
Calculate extension = new length - original length and force = weight = mg.
Plot a graph of force against extension and draw a line of best fit.
Spring constant = gradient of the straight-line section.
Accuracy: read at eye level, wait for the spring to stop moving, repeat and average, do not exceed the limit of proportionality.
exam.tip: Six-mark method: equipment, measurements, calculation, graph, k, improvements.

worked.q: A student hangs a 300 g mass on a spring. The spring extends from 8.0 cm to 14.0 cm. Calculate the spring constant. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: Force = weight = m x g = 0.300 x 10 = 3.0 N.

worked.q: A catapult has a spring constant of 500 N/m and is pulled back by 12 cm (within its limit of proportionality). Calculate the force needed and the energy stored.
steps: Force F = k x = 500 x 0.12 = 60 N.
Check with area: 0.5 x 60 x 0.12 = 3.6 J.

worked.q: A force-extension graph is a straight line from (0 m, 0 N) to (0.08 m, 4.0 N). Find k and the work done to stretch it 0.08 m.
steps: Gradient = change in force / change in extension = 4.0 / 0.08 = 50 N/m.
Work done = area of triangle = 0.5 x 0.08 x 4.0.

phy_ocra.5.2.summary: **All matter has a gravitational field** that attracts other masses, but the field is only noticeably strong around very **massive objects** such as planets, moons and stars. An object's **weight** is the **gravitational force** on it, measured in newtons with a **newtonmeter**, and is linked to mass by **weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = mg)**. Near the Earth's surface g is about **10 N/kg**, which is also the **acceleration of an object in free fall, about 10 m/s^2**. Mass stays the same everywhere, but weight changes if g changes, for example on the Moon.

core.p: A **gravitational field** is the region around a mass where another mass feels a force of attraction. **All matter** has a gravitational field, including you and this page, but the force between everyday objects is far too small to notice. Only very massive objects such as the Earth, the Moon and the Sun produce fields strong enough to matter.
bullets: Gravity is a **non-contact force**: it acts at a distance.
Gravity is always **attractive**; it never repels.
The greater the mass of the object, the stronger its gravitational field.
The field gets weaker with increasing distance from the object.
Earth's field pulls objects towards the **centre of the Earth**.

callouts.p: All matter has a gravitational field that causes attraction, and the field strength is much greater for massive objects.

core.p: **Gravitational field strength (g)** is the force of gravity acting on each kilogram of mass, measured in **newtons per kilogram (N/kg)**. Near the Earth's surface g is about **10 N/kg** (more precisely 9.8 N/kg). Other planets and moons have different values because they have different masses and radii.
bullets: g = weight / mass, unit N/kg.
Earth's surface: g = 10 N/kg (use the value given in the question).
Moon's surface: g is about 1.6 N/kg, roughly one sixth of Earth's.
Jupiter: g is about 25 N/kg, because Jupiter is far more massive.
g decreases as you move further from the planet's centre.

callouts.p: The force per unit mass acting on an object in a gravitational field, measured in N/kg.

core.p: **Mass** is the **amount of matter** in an object, measured in **kilograms (kg)**. It is a scalar and **does not change** with location. **Weight** is the **force** of gravity on the object, measured in **newtons (N)**. It is a vector, acts towards the centre of the planet, and **changes** if g changes.
bullets: An astronaut has the same mass on Earth and on the Moon.
The astronaut's weight on the Moon is about one sixth of their weight on Earth.
In everyday speech people say weight in kg; in physics weight is always in N.
Weight acts from the object's **centre of mass**.

callouts.p: The force acting on an object due to gravity; it is measured in newtons.
Never give weight in kg. Kilograms are for mass; newtons are for weight.

core.p: Weight, mass and gravitational field strength are linked by one equation. Weight is **directly proportional** to mass: double the mass, double the weight, in the same field.
bullets: weight (N) = mass (kg) x gravitational field strength (N/kg).
W = m g.
Rearranged: m = W / g and g = W / m.
Convert grams to kilograms first (divide by 1000).
A graph of weight against mass is a straight line through the origin with gradient g.

callouts.p: weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = mg)

core.p: Weight is measured using a **newtonmeter** (also called a **spring balance** or force meter). It contains a spring that stretches when an object hangs from it; the extension is proportional to the force, so the scale can be marked in newtons.
bullets: Zero the newtonmeter before use.
Hang the object from the hook and let it come to rest.
Read the scale at eye level to avoid parallax error.
Choose a newtonmeter with a suitable range and resolution.
Mass is measured with a balance; weight can then be calculated using W = mg.

callouts.p: If asked how to measure weight, name the instrument (newtonmeter) and the unit (N).

core.p: A simple experiment shows weight is proportional to mass and lets you find g. Measure the mass of several objects on a balance, measure their weights with a newtonmeter, then plot weight against mass.
bullets: Independent variable: mass (kg). Dependent variable: weight (N).
Plot weight on the y-axis and mass on the x-axis.
Expect a straight line through the origin: direct proportion.
Gradient = weight / mass = g, about 10 N/kg on Earth.
Repeat readings and take a mean to improve accuracy.

core.p: An object is in **free fall** when the **only force acting on it is its weight** (gravity). The resultant force is its weight, so by Newton's second law it accelerates downwards. Near the Earth's surface, the acceleration in free fall is about **10 m/s^2**, the same for every object regardless of mass, if air resistance is negligible.
bullets: Acceleration in free fall near Earth's surface is about 10 m/s^2 (9.8 m/s^2).
g in N/kg is numerically equal to free-fall acceleration in m/s^2.
Every second, a freely falling object gains about 10 m/s of speed.
Heavy and light objects fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

callouts.p: The acceleration in free fall near the Earth's surface is approximately 10 m/s^2.
Motion of an object when the only force acting on it is gravity (its weight).

core.h: Why all objects fall at the same rate
core.p: A heavier object has a bigger weight, but it also has more mass to accelerate. Using F = ma with F = mg gives mg = ma, so a = g. The mass cancels, so **every object has the same free-fall acceleration**.
bullets: Double the mass: double the weight, but also double the inertia.
So the acceleration stays the same: a = W / m = g.
In air, a feather falls slower because air resistance is large compared with its tiny weight.
On the Moon (no atmosphere) a hammer and feather land together.

callouts.p: Heavier objects do not fall faster in free fall. Any difference in real life is due to air resistance.

core.p: Gravitational field strength depends on **how massive** the object is and **how far away** you are from it. This is why the Sun, despite being far away, keeps the planets in orbit, while the attraction between two people is undetectable.
bullets: More mass: stronger field.
Greater distance: weaker field.
Astronauts in orbit still have weight; they feel weightless because they are in continuous free fall.
Gravity holds planets in orbit around the Sun and the Moon in orbit around the Earth.

core.h: Weight and gravitational potential energy links
core.p: Weight is the force you work against when lifting. Lifting an object at steady speed needs a force equal to its weight, so the work done is weight x height. This is why the gravitational potential energy equation contains m and g together (covered in the energy topic).
bullets: Work done lifting = weight x vertical height = m g h.
On the Moon the same lift needs less work because g is smaller.
Weight always acts vertically downwards towards the centre of the planet.

core.p: Six-mark questions often ask you to compare mass and weight or explain what happens on another planet. Structure answers: define each quantity, give units and instruments, then explain how g affects weight but not mass, with a calculation if data are given.
bullets: Define mass (amount of matter, kg) and weight (gravitational force, N).
State W = mg.
Explain that g depends on the mass of the planet.
Mass is unchanged; weight is proportional to g.
Use figures: e.g. 70 kg gives 700 N on Earth, 112 N on the Moon.

callouts.p: When a question gives a different value of g, use it; do not automatically use 10 N/kg.

analogy.t: Mass is the suitcase, weight is how hard it is to hold
analogy.p: Your mass is like the contents of a suitcase: the amount of stuff inside never changes wherever you take it. Your weight is like how hard the suitcase pulls on your arm, which depends on how strong the local gravitational field is. On the Moon the same suitcase is much easier to hold, even though nothing has been taken out. Where it breaks down: the effort to hold a suitcase also involves your muscles and the handle, while weight is purely the gravitational force; and mass also affects how hard it is to accelerate the case sideways, which does not change on the Moon.

terms.d: A region in which a mass experiences a force due to another mass.
The attractive non-contact force between any two masses.
Force per unit mass in a gravitational field, in N/kg; about 10 N/kg at Earth's surface.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kg; does not change with location.
The force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons.
The unit of force.
A spring-based instrument used to measure force, including weight, in newtons.
Falling when the only force acting is gravity.
The acceleration of a freely falling object, about 10 m/s^2 near Earth.
A force that acts between objects that are not touching, e.g. gravity.
The point at which the weight of an object can be taken to act.
Two quantities where doubling one doubles the other; e.g. weight and mass.
A frictional force opposing motion through air.
The single force with the same effect as all the forces on an object.

mistakes.r: Mass stays the same; only weight changes.

mistakes.r: The Moon has a weaker gravitational field, about 1.6 N/kg.

mistakes.r: In free fall all objects have the same acceleration, about 10 m/s^2.

mistakes.r: All matter has a gravitational field; it is just very weak for small masses.

exam.q: State the unit of gravitational field strength.
model: N/kg (newtons per kilogram).
exam.tip: Not m/s, not N.

exam.q: Define weight.
model: The force acting on an object due to gravity.
exam.tip: Must say force.

exam.q: State the acceleration of an object in free fall near the Earth's surface.
model: About 10 m/s^2 (accept 9.8 m/s^2).
exam.tip: Include unit.

exam.q: Calculate the weight of a 2.5 kg bag on Earth. (g = 10 N/kg)
exam.tip: Show the equation.

exam.q: Name the instrument used to measure weight and give the unit of the reading.
model: Newtonmeter / spring balance / force meter.
Newtons (N).
exam.tip: Two separate marks.

exam.q: Explain why the gravitational attraction between two people is not noticeable but the attraction between a person and the Earth is.
model: All masses attract but the force is tiny for small masses.
The Earth has a very large mass so its gravitational field is strong.
exam.tip: Link field strength to mass.

exam.q: A rock weighs 48 N on the Moon where g = 1.6 N/kg. Calculate its mass and its weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
model: m = 30 kg.
W on Earth = 30 x 10.
exam.tip: Mass is the bridge between the two planets.

exam.q: Explain why a hammer and a feather dropped together on the Moon land at the same time.
model: There is no atmosphere / no air resistance on the Moon.
The only force is weight, so both are in free fall.
Free-fall acceleration is the same for all masses (a = g).
exam.tip: Mention both no air resistance and same acceleration.

exam.q: Describe how a student could show that weight is proportional to mass.
model: Measure masses of several objects using a balance.
Measure their weights using a newtonmeter.
Plot a graph of weight against mass.
A straight line through the origin shows direct proportion (gradient = g).
exam.tip: Include the graph conclusion.

exam.q: Compare the mass and weight of an astronaut on Earth and on the Moon. Use W = mg in your answer.
model: Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the gravitational force (N).
Mass does not change with location, so it is the same on the Moon.
W = m x g, so weight depends on g.
The Moon has less mass than Earth, so its gravitational field strength is smaller (about 1.6 N/kg vs 10 N/kg).
So the astronaut's weight on the Moon is about one sixth of that on Earth.
E.g. 80 kg astronaut: 800 N on Earth, 128 N on the Moon; mass is 80 kg in both places.
exam.tip: Use a numerical example to secure the top marks.

worked.q: A student has a mass of 55 kg. Calculate their weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) and on Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg).
steps: Mass is still 55 kg on Mars.
Weight on Mars is about 0.37 times weight on Earth.
worked.ans: 550 N on Earth, about 204 N on Mars; mass 55 kg in both places.

worked.q: An apple of mass 150 g falls from a tree. Calculate its weight and its acceleration, ignoring air resistance (g = 10 N/kg).
steps: The only force is weight, so resultant force = 1.5 N.
This equals g, as expected for free fall.

worked.q: A newtonmeter reads 7.4 N when a 2.0 kg object hangs from it on an unknown planet. Find g on that planet.
steps: This is about the value for Mars.
Free-fall acceleration there would be 3.7 m/s^2.

phy_ocra.5.3.summary: Mass, weight and gravitational field strength are linked by **W = m x g**. Mass is the amount of matter in an object and stays the same everywhere, but weight is a force that changes whenever g changes, for example on another planet or far from the Earth's surface. For triple you must be able to predict and explain how a change in one of these quantities affects the others, including the effects on gravitational potential energy (GPE = m x g x h) and on the acceleration of a falling object.

core.h: The key equation: W = m x g
core.p: **Weight** is the gravitational force acting on an object's mass. It is found by multiplying the mass by the **gravitational field strength** at that place. Because it is a force, weight is measured in newtons and acts towards the centre of the planet.
bullets: **weight (N) = mass (kg) x gravitational field strength (N/kg)**
Rearranged: m = W / g and g = W / m
Weight is **directly proportional** to mass when g is constant: double the mass, double the weight
Weight is **directly proportional** to g when mass is constant: double g, double the weight
On Earth, g is about **10 N/kg** (9.8 N/kg more precisely); OCR gives the value in the question

callouts.p: The force acting on an object due to gravity, equal to mass x gravitational field strength, measured in newtons (N).
Mass in kg, weight in N, gravitational field strength in N/kg. Always convert grams to kilograms first.

core.p: Mass is a measure of how much matter an object contains and how hard it is to change its motion (its **inertia**). Moving an object to the Moon does not add or remove any particles, so its mass is **unchanged**. But the Moon pulls less strongly, so its weight is smaller.
bullets: Mass is a **scalar**; weight is a **vector** (it has a direction: towards the centre of the planet)
Mass measured with a balance (comparing masses); weight measured with a **newtonmeter** (spring balance)
A 60 kg astronaut has mass 60 kg on Earth, the Moon and in deep space
Their weight is about 600 N on Earth, about 96 N on the Moon and nearly 0 N far from any planet
Kitchen scales read in kg but really measure the force on them, so they would give the wrong mass on the Moon

callouts.p: People say 'I weigh 60 kg'. In physics that is their mass. Their weight is about 600 N.

core.h: What sets the value of g?
core.p: The gravitational field strength of a planet depends on its **mass** and on how far you are from its **centre**. A more massive planet produces a stronger field; moving further away makes the field weaker.
bullets: Larger planet mass gives **larger g** at the surface
Greater distance from the centre gives **smaller g**
g does **not** depend on the mass of the object placed in the field
Earth about 10 N/kg, Moon about 1.6 N/kg, Mars about 3.7 N/kg, Jupiter about 25 N/kg
On top of a high mountain g is very slightly less than at sea level, because you are further from Earth's centre

callouts.p: g is a property of the gravitational field at a location, not of the object in it.

core.h: g as a force per kilogram
core.p: Rearranging W = m x g gives g = W / m. This shows what gravitational field strength really means: **the force of gravity on each kilogram of mass**. On Earth every kilogram is pulled with about 10 N.
bullets: g = 10 N/kg means each 1 kg feels 10 N of weight
This is why the unit is **N/kg**
A field with g = 1.6 N/kg (Moon) pulls each kilogram with 1.6 N
You can find g for an unknown planet by hanging a known mass on a newtonmeter and dividing the reading by the mass

callouts.p: The force per unit mass acting on a mass placed in a gravitational field, measured in N/kg.

core.p: If weight is the only force acting (free fall, no air resistance), Newton's second law gives a = F / m = (m x g) / m = **g**. So g is also the acceleration of free fall, and 10 N/kg is the same as 10 m/s squared.
bullets: The mass **cancels out**, so all objects fall with the same acceleration when only gravity acts
A heavier object has a bigger weight, but also a bigger mass to accelerate, in exactly the same ratio
On the Moon (no air) a hammer and a feather dropped together land at the same time
On Earth they do not, because **air resistance** has a much bigger effect on the light feather
Units: N/kg = (kg m/s squared)/kg = m/s squared

callouts.p: Say: double the mass gives double the weight, but double the mass needs double the force for the same acceleration, so the acceleration stays the same.

core.h: Changing mass at a fixed g
core.p: In one place g is fixed, so weight changes in direct proportion to mass. A graph of weight against mass is a **straight line through the origin** and its **gradient equals g**.
bullets: Add a second identical mass: weight doubles
Halve the mass: weight halves
Gradient of a weight-mass graph = W / m = g
A steeper line means a stronger gravitational field
Useful for comparing planets on one set of axes

core.h: Changing g at a fixed mass
core.p: Take the same object to different places: its mass is fixed, so its weight is directly proportional to g. To compare, use the ratio of the field strengths.
bullets: New weight = old weight x (new g / old g)
Earth to Moon: weight multiplied by 1.6/10 = 0.16, about one sixth
Earth to Jupiter: weight multiplied by 2.5
This is why astronauts can jump higher on the Moon: their legs push the same mass against a much smaller weight

callouts.p: In 'what happens on the Moon' questions, the mass stays the same. Only weight and anything that depends on g change.

core.p: Gravitational potential energy depends on g too: **GPE = m x g x h**. So the energy needed to lift an object through a height also changes from planet to planet.
bullets: GPE (J) = mass (kg) x gravitational field strength (N/kg) x height (m)
Lifting 2 kg by 1 m on Earth stores 20 J; on the Moon only 3.2 J
Same mass and height but smaller g means **less work done** lifting
GPE is proportional to each of m, g and h, so doubling any one doubles the GPE
Weight x height is the same as m x g x h: the work done against weight

callouts.p: Work done = force x distance = weight x height = m x g x h, which equals the gain in GPE.

core.h: Linked changes to falling and landing
core.p: When an object falls, GPE transfers to kinetic energy. Because both the weight and the GPE depend on g, a change of planet changes how fast an object is moving when it lands.
bullets: With no air resistance, loss in GPE = gain in KE: m x g x h = 0.5 x m x v squared
Mass cancels again, so landing speed depends only on g and h
Smaller g gives a **smaller acceleration** and a **slower landing speed** from the same height
Smaller g also means the fall takes **longer**

core.p: Exam questions often give one change and ask you to predict the others. Work through which quantity is a property of the object (mass) and which is a property of the place (g).
bullets: Identify what stays constant first
Then use W = m x g or GPE = m x g x h as a proportion
State the direction of change and the factor (for example, 'weight decreases to about one sixth')

callouts.p: Higher-mark answers quote the factor: 'weight is 0.16 times as large', not just 'weight is smaller'.

core.p: Far out in space the gravitational field strength becomes tiny, so an object's weight becomes almost zero while its mass is unchanged. It still has the same inertia, so it is just as hard to push it into motion or stop it.
bullets: Pushing a massive object in deep space still needs a large force to give it a large acceleration (F = m x a)
Mass resists changes in motion even when weight is near zero
Gravity's effect gets weaker with distance but never quite reaches zero

callouts.t: Zero weight is not zero mass
callouts.p: An astronaut far from Earth is not 'massless'; they still have all their mass and inertia.

analogy.t: Mass is your bag, g is the conveyor's slope
analogy.p: Think of mass as the contents of a suitcase, which you pack once and never change. The gravitational field strength is like how steep the slope is where you put it down: on a steep slope (big g, like Jupiter) the suitcase pulls hard on the handle, on a gentle slope (small g, like the Moon) it pulls gently. The pull on the handle is the weight. It breaks down because a slope only pulls a suitcase along one direction you choose, whereas gravity always pulls towards a planet's centre, and gravity acts on every particle without needing contact.

terms.d: The amount of matter in an object; a measure of its inertia; measured in kg; the same everywhere.
The gravitational force on an object; weight = mass x gravitational field strength; measured in N.
The force per unit mass on an object in a gravitational field, measured in N/kg.
The region around a mass where another mass feels a force of attraction.
The unit of force; 1 N gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s squared.
A spring-based instrument used to measure force, including weight.
The tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion; depends on mass.
Motion where weight is the only force acting on an object.
The acceleration of an object in free fall, numerically equal to g (about 10 m/s squared on Earth).
Energy stored because of an object's position in a gravitational field; GPE = m x g x h.
Two quantities where doubling one doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
A quantity with size only, such as mass.
A quantity with size and direction, such as weight.
A frictional force on a moving object from the air, acting opposite to its motion.

mistakes.w: The astronaut's mass is less on the Moon.
mistakes.r: Mass is unchanged; only weight decreases because g is smaller.

mistakes.w: Weight is measured in kilograms.
mistakes.r: Weight is a force measured in newtons; mass is in kilograms.

mistakes.w: Heavier objects fall faster because they have more weight.
mistakes.r: Weight and mass increase in the same ratio, so the acceleration (g) is the same when only gravity acts.

mistakes.w: g depends on the mass of the object.
mistakes.r: g depends on the planet's mass and the distance from its centre, not on the object.

mistakes.w: Using grams in W = m x g, e.g. 500 x 10 = 5000 N.
mistakes.r: Convert to kg first: 0.5 x 10 = 5 N.

mistakes.w: In space there is no gravity so objects have no mass.
mistakes.r: Far from planets g is very small so weight is near zero, but mass and inertia are unchanged.

mistakes.w: The weight is smaller on the Moon because there is no air.
mistakes.r: Weight is smaller because the Moon has less mass, so its gravitational field strength is smaller.

mistakes.w: Weight is smaller on the Moon, so GPE is the same.
mistakes.r: GPE = m x g x h, so a smaller g gives a smaller GPE for the same mass and height.

exam.q: State the equation that links weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
model: weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = m x g)
exam.tip: Write words or standard symbols; do not invent symbols.

exam.q: An object has a mass of 4 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
model: W = 40 N
exam.tip: Always give the unit, N.

exam.q: Explain the difference between mass and weight.
model: Mass is the amount of matter in an object and is the same everywhere / measured in kg
Weight is the force of gravity on the mass, which depends on g / measured in N
exam.tip: Make one point about each quantity.

exam.q: A rover has a weight of 1850 N on Mars, where g = 3.7 N/kg. Calculate its mass.
model: m = W / g
m = 500 kg
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: The rover in the previous question is taken to Earth (g = 10 N/kg). State and explain what happens to its mass and its weight.
model: Mass stays the same (500 kg) because the amount of matter does not change
Weight increases because g is larger on Earth
New weight = 500 x 10 = 5000 N
exam.tip: Treat mass and weight separately and give a reason for each.

exam.q: Suggest why the gravitational field strength on Jupiter is greater than on Earth.
model: Jupiter has a much greater mass than Earth
exam.tip: Link g to the planet's mass.

exam.q: A hammer and a feather are dropped together on the Moon and land at the same time. Explain why.
model: There is no air on the Moon, so there is no air resistance
Weight is the only force acting on each object
The hammer has a bigger weight but also a bigger mass
Acceleration = weight / mass = g, which is the same for both
exam.tip: Mention both the force and the mass, then conclude with a = g.

exam.q: An astronaut has a weight of 720 N on Earth (g = 10 N/kg). Calculate her weight on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg).
model: weight on Moon = 72 x 1.6
exam.tip: Find the mass first because mass does not change.

exam.q: A 2 kg box is lifted 3 m on Earth and the same box is lifted 3 m on the Moon. Compare the GPE gained in each case. (Earth g = 10 N/kg, Moon g = 1.6 N/kg)
model: Earth: GPE = 2 x 10 x 3 = 60 J
Moon: GPE = 2 x 1.6 x 3 = 9.6 J
Less GPE is gained on the Moon
Because g is smaller, so the weight lifted is smaller and less work is done
exam.tip: Calculate both, then compare in words.

exam.q: A student hangs different masses from a newtonmeter on an unknown planet and plots weight against mass. Describe how the student can use the graph to find g, and explain how the graph would differ on Earth.
model: Plot weight (N) on the y-axis against mass (kg) on the x-axis
The points form a straight line through the origin, showing weight is proportional to mass
Draw a line of best fit
Calculate the gradient = change in weight / change in mass
The gradient equals g in N/kg
If the planet has a smaller g than Earth, Earth's line would be steeper (larger gradient)
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need method, what the graph shows, how to get g, and a comparison.

worked.q: A satellite has a mass of 800 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth (g = 9.8 N/kg) and at a height where g = 2.5 N/kg.
steps: Mass is the same at both places: m = 800 kg
On Earth: W = m x g = 800 x 9.8 = 7840 N
worked.ans: 7840 N on Earth and 2000 N at the height; the mass stays 800 kg.

worked.q: A ball is dropped from 5 m on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) and on Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg). Ignoring air resistance, find its landing speed in each case.
steps: Loss of GPE = gain of KE: m x g x h = 0.5 x m x v squared
Mass cancels: v squared = 2 x g x h
Earth: v squared = 2 x 10 x 5 = 100, so v = 10 m/s
Mars: v squared = 2 x 3.7 x 5 = 37, so v = 6.1 m/s
worked.ans: 10 m/s on Earth and about 6.1 m/s on Mars; the smaller g gives a slower landing.

phy_ocra.5.4.summary: A force can make an object turn about a pivot, and the turning effect is called a **moment**: moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. When an object is balanced, the **principle of moments** says the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment. Levers and gears use moments to transmit rotational effects, letting a small force produce a large turning effect (force multiplier) or changing speed and direction of rotation.

core.p: A force applied at a distance from a **pivot** (fulcrum) makes an object rotate. Everyday examples include opening a door, turning a spanner, using a see-saw, a wheelbarrow, scissors, a bottle opener and pedalling a bike.
bullets: A door turns about its **hinges**: push far from the hinge and it opens easily
A spanner turns a nut: a longer spanner gives a bigger turning effect for the same force
A see-saw turns about its central pivot
A force whose line of action passes **through the pivot** produces **no** turning effect
Turning can be **clockwise** or **anticlockwise**

callouts.p: The fixed point about which an object turns; also called the fulcrum.

core.p: The size of the turning effect depends on **two things**: how big the force is and how far from the pivot it acts. The distance must be the **perpendicular distance** from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
bullets: **moment of a force (Nm) = force (N) x distance (m)**
The distance is measured at **right angles** to the force
Bigger force gives a bigger moment
Bigger perpendicular distance gives a bigger moment
Unit: **newton metre (Nm)**; if distance is in cm, the moment is in Ncm
Pushing at an angle to a door reduces the perpendicular distance, so reduces the moment

callouts.p: The turning effect of a force about a pivot, equal to the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
Moments are in newton metres (Nm). Do not write joules, even though work done also multiplies force by distance.

core.p: Always convert distances to metres if the question asks for Nm. Then multiply force by perpendicular distance.
bullets: A 20 N force at 0.3 m from a pivot: moment = 20 x 0.3 = 6 Nm
Rearranged: force = moment / distance; distance = moment / force
To get the same moment with half the distance you need twice the force
Weight acts from the object's **centre of mass**, so use the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass

callouts.p: Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with Nm. Most marks come from correct substitution.

core.p: If an object is **balanced** (in equilibrium and not turning), the turning effects in the two directions cancel out.
bullets: **Sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments** about any pivot
Add up all the moments in each direction separately, then set them equal
If the clockwise total is larger, the object turns clockwise
Used to find an unknown force or an unknown distance on a balanced beam
For balance, there must also be no resultant force: the pivot pushes up to balance the weights

callouts.p: For an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a pivot is equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that pivot.

core.p: Write each side as force x distance. Put the unknown on one side and solve. Check that your answer makes sense: the smaller force must be further from the pivot.
bullets: Anticlockwise: F1 x d1; Clockwise: F2 x d2
Balanced: F1 x d1 = F2 x d2
With several weights on one side: F1 x d1 + F2 x d2 = F3 x d3
A child of 300 N sits 2 m from the pivot; an adult of 600 N must sit 1 m from the pivot to balance
Heavier people sit closer to the pivot

callouts.p: A small force a long way from the pivot can balance a large force close to the pivot.

core.p: A **lever** is a rigid bar that turns about a pivot. You apply an **effort** to move a **load**. If the effort acts much further from the pivot than the load, a small effort produces a large moment, which can move a large load.
bullets: Moment of effort = moment of load (when just balancing)
Effort x distance of effort from pivot = load x distance of load from pivot
Longer handle means less effort is needed: a **force multiplier**
Examples: crowbar, wheelbarrow, nutcracker, claw hammer, spanner, bottle opener
The trade-off: the effort must move through a **larger distance** than the load
Energy is not created: work done by effort is at least equal to work done on load

head: Lever
Where is the pivot?
Effect
rows: Effort between pivot and load; large movement of load

callouts.p: State that the effort is further from the pivot, so a smaller force gives the same moment as the load.

core.p: A metre rule is balanced on a pivot at its centre. Known masses are hung at measured distances on each side and moved until the rule balances. The moments on each side are then calculated and compared.
bullets: Balance the metre rule at its centre first so its own weight has no moment
Hang masses using loops of thread; read distances from the pivot to the thread
Weight = mass x g, converting grams to kilograms
Calculate clockwise and anticlockwise moments and show they are (nearly) equal
Repeat with different masses and distances
Sources of error: thread slipping, reading the scale at an angle (parallax), friction at the pivot

callouts.p: Use a knife-edge pivot to reduce friction and read distances at eye level to avoid parallax error.

core.p: **Gears** are toothed wheels that interlock. When one gear turns, its teeth push the teeth of the next gear, transmitting the rotational effect. Adjacent gears turn in **opposite directions**.
bullets: The force between the teeth is the same size on both gears at the contact point
Moment = force x radius, so a **larger gear** experiences a **larger moment**
A small driving gear turning a larger gear: output moment increases, output speed decreases
A large driving gear turning a smaller gear: output turns faster but with a smaller moment
Example: low gears on a bicycle make it easier to climb hills; a car's gearbox

callouts.p: Two meshing gears always rotate in opposite directions.

core.h: Why a bigger gear gives a bigger moment
core.p: At the point where the teeth meet, the force on the driven gear equals the force from the driving gear (Newton's third law). The driven gear has a bigger radius, so the same force acts at a bigger distance from its axle, giving a bigger moment.
bullets: Output moment / input moment = radius of driven gear / radius of driving gear
The number of teeth is proportional to the radius
A gear with twice the teeth turns at half the speed with twice the moment
Like levers, gears do not give extra energy: a bigger moment comes with slower rotation

callouts.t: Gears do not give free energy
callouts.p: Saying a gear 'creates more force' is not enough. Explain that the moment is bigger because the same force acts at a larger radius.

core.p: The weight of an object acts through its centre of mass, so it can create a moment about the edge of its base. If the line of action of the weight falls outside the base, the weight produces a moment that topples the object.
bullets: A wide base and a low centre of mass make an object more stable
Tilted until the weight acts outside the base, a resultant moment tips it over
Cranes use counterweights so the moments balance about the tower

core.p: Moments questions reward a clear structure: identify the pivot, identify each force and its perpendicular distance, decide clockwise or anticlockwise, then apply the principle of moments.
bullets: Draw or label the pivot on the diagram
Mark each force as clockwise or anticlockwise
Convert units consistently (all in m or all in cm)
Check: the answer should make physical sense

callouts.p: If all distances are in cm you can keep them in cm for a balance problem, since the units cancel when finding a force.

analogy.t: Pushing a door is like a see-saw of effort
analogy.p: Opening a heavy door near the hinge feels like trying to lift a friend on a see-saw while sitting right next to the pivot: hopeless. Move out to the handle, the far end of the see-saw, and the same push suddenly has a big turning effect. The analogy maps force x distance well. It breaks down because a door usually has no load on the other side trying to balance it; the resistance comes from the door's inertia and friction in the hinges, not an opposing moment from a second person.

terms.d: The turning effect of a force: force x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
The point about which an object rotates.
The shortest distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, at right angles to the force.
The straight line along which a force acts.
The unit of moment.
A moment that tends to turn an object in the same direction as the hands of a clock.
A moment that tends to turn an object in the opposite direction to the hands of a clock.
For a balanced object, total clockwise moment about a pivot = total anticlockwise moment about that pivot.
The state of an object with no resultant force and no resultant moment acting on it.
A rigid bar that turns about a pivot, used to transmit the rotational effect of a force.
The force applied to a lever or machine.
The force that a lever or machine works against or moves.
A device such as a lever that allows a small effort to move a larger load.
A toothed wheel that interlocks with another to transmit a rotational effect.
The point through which the weight of an object can be taken to act.

mistakes.w: Moment = force x distance in J.
mistakes.r: Moments are measured in Nm (newton metres).

mistakes.w: Using the distance along the bar when the force acts at an angle.
mistakes.r: Use the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.

mistakes.w: A balanced beam has equal forces on each side.
mistakes.r: It has equal clockwise and anticlockwise moments; forces can differ if distances differ.

mistakes.w: Mixing cm and m, e.g. 20 N x 30 cm = 600 Nm.
mistakes.r: Convert: 30 cm = 0.3 m, so the moment is 6 Nm.

mistakes.w: A lever reduces the work you have to do.
mistakes.r: A lever reduces the force needed, but the effort moves through a larger distance; the work done is not reduced.

mistakes.w: Meshing gears turn in the same direction.
mistakes.r: Adjacent gears turn in opposite directions.

mistakes.w: A bigger gear turns faster.
mistakes.r: When a small gear drives a bigger gear, the bigger gear turns more slowly but with a larger moment.

mistakes.w: Using the mass in grams as the force in a moment calculation.
mistakes.r: Convert mass to kg and multiply by g to find the weight in N first.

exam.q: State the equation linking moment, force and distance.
model: moment = force x (perpendicular) distance (from the pivot)
exam.tip: Add 'perpendicular' and 'from the pivot' for full precision.

exam.q: A force of 15 N acts 0.4 m from a pivot. Calculate the moment.
model: moment = 15 x 0.4
= 6 Nm
exam.tip: Give the unit Nm.

exam.q: Explain why it is easier to undo a tight nut with a long spanner than a short one.
model: The force acts at a greater distance from the pivot (nut)
So a smaller force produces the same (or a larger) moment
exam.tip: Link distance to moment.

exam.q: State the principle of moments.
model: For a balanced object / in equilibrium
Total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment (about the same pivot)
exam.tip: Both conditions earn a mark each.

exam.q: A 400 N child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a see-saw. How far from the pivot must a 600 N adult sit on the other side to balance it?
exam.tip: Set clockwise equal to anticlockwise.

exam.q: A metre rule is pivoted at its centre. A 2 N weight hangs 30 cm to the left of the pivot and a 3 N weight hangs 10 cm to the left. What force is needed 40 cm to the right to balance it?
model: Anticlockwise moments = (2 x 30) + (3 x 10) = 90 Ncm
Clockwise moment = F x 40
exam.tip: Add moments on the same side before equating.

exam.q: Explain how a crowbar allows a person to lift a heavy rock with a small force.
model: The effort is applied much further from the pivot than the load
The moment of the effort equals force x a large distance
So a small effort produces a moment equal to the large load x small distance
exam.tip: Use the words pivot, effort, load and moment.

exam.q: A small gear with 10 teeth drives a larger gear with 30 teeth. State and explain two differences in how the large gear rotates compared with the small gear.
model: The large gear turns in the opposite direction
The large gear turns more slowly (one third the speed)
The large gear has a larger moment (three times)
Because the same force at the teeth acts at a larger radius
exam.tip: Give the direction, speed and moment, with a reason for the moment.

exam.q: Describe how a student could use a metre rule, a pivot, masses and thread to verify the principle of moments.
model: Balance the metre rule on a pivot at its 50 cm mark
Hang a known mass on one side and measure its distance from the pivot
Hang a second mass on the other side and adjust its position until the rule balances
Calculate weights using W = m x g
Calculate the moment on each side (force x distance)
Repeat for different masses/positions; clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal within experimental error
exam.tip: Structure: set-up, measurements, calculation, repeat, conclusion.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of moments, why a bicycle in a low gear is easier to pedal up a hill.
model: In a low gear the rear gear (sprocket) is larger compared with the front gear
So the same force from the chain gives a larger moment on the rear wheel
exam.tip: Mention the bigger driven gear radius.

worked.q: A uniform beam is pivoted at its centre. A 50 N load hangs 0.8 m to the left of the pivot. A 20 N load hangs 0.5 m to the right. Where must a 30 N load be placed on the right to balance the beam?
worked.ans: The 30 N load must hang 1.0 m to the right of the pivot.

worked.q: A wheelbarrow carries a load of 600 N whose centre of mass is 0.4 m from the wheel axle. The handles are 1.2 m from the axle. What upward force is needed at the handles to just lift the load?
steps: The pivot is the wheel axle
Balance: F x 1.2 = 240, so F = 200 N
worked.ans: 200 N, one third of the load, because the effort acts three times as far from the pivot.
