phy_ocra.5.5.summary: Pressure is the force acting normal to a surface per unit area: **pressure = force / area**. In a fluid (a liquid or gas), pressure acts in all directions and at right angles to any surface, and in a liquid it increases with depth and density: **pressure = height x density x g**. Hydraulic systems use the fact that pressure is transmitted equally through a liquid to turn a small force on a small piston into a large force on a large piston. The difference in pressure between the top and bottom of an object causes upthrust, which decides whether it floats or sinks, and the weight of the air above us causes atmospheric pressure, which decreases with height.

core.p: Pressure tells you how concentrated a force is. The same force spread over a big area gives a low pressure; concentrated on a small area it gives a high pressure.
bullets: **pressure (Pa) = force normal to a surface (N) / area of that surface (m squared)**
1 pascal (Pa) = 1 N/m squared
Rearranged: force = pressure x area
Sharp knives and drawing pins have a tiny area so produce a large pressure
Snow shoes, tractor tyres and wide straps spread force over a large area to reduce pressure
Convert cm squared to m squared by dividing by 10 000

callouts.p: The force acting normal (at right angles) to a surface divided by the area of that surface.
1 m squared = 10 000 cm squared, not 100 cm squared.

core.h: Pressure in fluids acts in all directions
core.p: A **fluid** is a liquid or a gas. Its particles move randomly and collide with every surface they touch. These collisions produce a force **at right angles (normal) to the surface**, in every direction.
bullets: Fluid pressure acts **normal to any surface** in contact with the fluid
At a given depth, the pressure is the same in all directions
Water squirts out at right angles from holes in a container
Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls

callouts.p: The force from fluid pressure always acts at 90 degrees to the surface.

core.p: The deeper you go in a liquid, the more liquid there is above you pushing down. So the pressure due to the liquid increases with depth. Denser liquids produce more pressure at the same depth.
bullets: **pressure due to a column of liquid (Pa) = height of column (m) x density of liquid (kg/m cubed) x g (N/kg)**
p = h x rho x g
Pressure is **proportional to depth**: double the depth, double the pressure
Pressure depends on depth and density, not on the shape or width of the container
Dams are thicker at the bottom because the water pressure is greatest there
Divers feel pressure on their ears increase as they descend

callouts.p: p = h x rho x g is a Higher tier equation; you must be able to recall and apply it.

core.p: Imagine a column of liquid of area A and height h above a point. Its mass is density x volume = rho x A x h, so its weight is rho x A x h x g. Pressure = weight / area = rho x h x g. The area cancels, which is why only depth and density matter.
bullets: Weight of column = mass x g = (rho x A x h) x g
Pressure = force / area = (rho x A x h x g) / A = h x rho x g
Total pressure underwater = atmospheric pressure + liquid pressure

core.p: Liquids are almost **incompressible**. When you push on a liquid in a closed system, the pressure increase is **transmitted equally** to all parts of the liquid. This is how hydraulic systems work.
bullets: Pressure at the small (input) piston = pressure at the large (output) piston
Input force / input area = output force / output area
A **small force on a small area** creates a pressure that produces a **large force on a large area**
Hydraulics are **force multipliers**
Examples: car brakes, hydraulic jacks, car lifts, diggers

callouts.p: F1 / A1 = F2 / A2, because the pressure is the same throughout the liquid.

core.p: Hydraulics do not give energy for free. The volume of liquid pushed out of the small cylinder equals the volume entering the large cylinder, so the small piston must move a long distance to move the large piston a short distance.
bullets: Volume moved = area x distance is the same on both sides
Work done on small piston = work done by large piston (ignoring friction)
Large output force, small output distance
Air bubbles in brake fluid are dangerous: air is compressible, so pressure is not transmitted well

callouts.p: A gas would compress when pushed, so the pressure would not be transmitted fully. Liquids are used because they are nearly incompressible.

core.p: An object in a fluid has more fluid pressure on its bottom surface than on its top surface, because the bottom is deeper. This difference produces a resultant upward force called **upthrust**.
bullets: Pressure on bottom face > pressure on top face
Upward force on bottom > downward force on top
Resultant upward force = upthrust
Upthrust is equal to the **weight of fluid displaced** by the object
Upthrust is larger in denser fluids and for objects that displace more fluid

callouts.p: The upward force on an object in a fluid, caused by the pressure being greater at the bottom of the object than at the top; equal to the weight of fluid displaced.

core.p: Whether something floats or sinks depends on how its weight compares with the upthrust it can get, which depends on its **density** compared with the fluid's density.
bullets: Upthrust equal to weight: object floats (forces balanced)
Weight greater than maximum upthrust: object sinks
Object less dense than the fluid: it floats
Object denser than the fluid: it sinks
A steel ship floats because its hollow shape displaces a large volume of water, so its average density is less than water
A floating object sinks into the fluid until the weight of fluid displaced equals its own weight

head: Situation
Forces
Result
rows: Density of object < density of fluid
Density of object > density of fluid

core.h: A simple model of the atmosphere
core.p: The atmosphere is a thin layer of air around the Earth, held by gravity. Air has weight, and the weight of the column of air above a surface causes **atmospheric pressure**, about 100 000 Pa at sea level.
bullets: Atmospheric pressure is caused by air particles colliding with surfaces
It acts in all directions, not just downwards
The atmosphere gets **less dense** with height
Higher up there is **less air above you**, so less weight of air
So atmospheric pressure **decreases with increasing height**
Climbers on high mountains find it harder to breathe; ears pop in aircraft

callouts.p: At greater altitude the column of air above is shorter and the air is less dense, so its weight per unit area is smaller.

core.p: Most fluid questions need one of three equations. Decide which by what you are given.
bullets: Force and area given: p = F / A
Depth and density given: p = h x rho x g
Two pistons: F1 / A1 = F2 / A2
Always check units: m, m squared, kg/m cubed, N, Pa
Give answers in Pa or kPa (1 kPa = 1000 Pa)

callouts.p: Output force = input force x (output area / input area). If the large piston has 50 times the area, the force is 50 times bigger.

core.p: Exam questions often set fluid pressure in a context. Explain using pressure, force and area each time.
bullets: Car braking: pedal pushes a small piston; pressure transmitted to large pistons at the wheels; large force on the brake pads
Hydraulic jack: small repeated pushes lift a car
Water towers: high height gives high pressure at taps
Submarines need thick hulls to withstand huge pressure at depth

analogy.p: Pressure in a liquid is like people squeezed into a sealed corridor. Push on the crowd at one narrow door and everyone pushes harder on every wall, so a wide door at the other end gets a big total push. And the people at the bottom of a pile feel the weight of everyone above, like deep water. The analogy breaks down because people can be squashed closer together, while a liquid is almost incompressible, and people push in chosen directions rather than randomly in all directions.

terms.d: Force normal to a surface divided by the area of the surface; unit Pa.
The unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m squared.
A substance that can flow: a liquid or a gas.
At right angles to a surface.
Mass per unit volume, measured in kg/m cubed.
Cannot be squashed into a smaller volume; liquids are almost incompressible.
A system that uses a liquid to transmit pressure from one piston to another.
A sliding disc or cylinder that a force acts on to change the pressure in a fluid.
A device that produces a larger output force than the input force.
The resultant upward force from a fluid on an object, equal to the weight of fluid displaced.
The fluid pushed out of the way by an object placed in it.
The pressure caused by the weight of the air above a surface; about 100 kPa at sea level.
The thin layer of air surrounding the Earth, held by gravity, becoming less dense with height.
The vertical distance below the surface of a fluid.

mistakes.w: Pressure in a liquid only acts downwards.
mistakes.r: Fluid pressure acts in all directions, at right angles to any surface.

mistakes.w: A wider container gives more pressure at the bottom.
mistakes.r: Pressure depends only on depth, density and g, not on width or shape.

mistakes.w: Hydraulics create extra energy.
mistakes.r: They multiply force, but the small piston moves further, so work done is not increased.

mistakes.w: Converting cm squared to m squared by dividing by 100.
mistakes.r: Divide by 10 000.

mistakes.w: Upthrust is caused by the water pushing up because it is heavy.
mistakes.r: Upthrust is caused by greater pressure on the bottom surface than on the top surface, as the bottom is deeper.

mistakes.w: Heavy objects sink and light objects float.
mistakes.r: Floating depends on density compared with the fluid: a heavy ship floats because its average density is less than water.

mistakes.w: Atmospheric pressure is lower on mountains because it is colder.
mistakes.r: It is lower because there is less air above and the air is less dense, so less weight of air pushes on each square metre.

mistakes.w: Gases are used in car brakes because they are light.
mistakes.r: Liquids are used because they are nearly incompressible, so pressure is transmitted.

exam.q: State the equation linking pressure, force and area.
model: pressure = force (normal to surface) / area
exam.tip: Include the units Pa, N and m squared if asked.

exam.q: A box with weight 600 N rests on an area of 0.2 m squared. Calculate the pressure on the floor.
exam.tip: Pa or N/m squared both earn the unit mark.

exam.q: Explain why a tractor has wide tyres.
model: Wide tyres give a large area in contact with the ground
So the pressure is reduced and the tractor does not sink into soft ground
exam.tip: Link area to pressure.

exam.q: Calculate the pressure due to water at a depth of 12 m. Density of water = 1000 kg/m cubed, g = 10 N/kg.
model: p = h x rho x g = 12 x 1000 x 10
exam.tip: Use the Higher tier equation.

exam.q: Explain why a dam is built thicker at the bottom than at the top.
model: Water pressure increases with depth
So the force on the bottom of the dam is greatest
exam.tip: Pressure and depth in one sentence.

exam.q: In a hydraulic jack, a force of 40 N acts on a piston of area 0.002 m squared. The output piston has an area of 0.1 m squared. Calculate the output force.
model: Pressure = 40 / 0.002 = 20 000 Pa
Same pressure on output piston
Output force = 20 000 x 0.1 = 2000 N
exam.tip: Find the pressure first, then use F = p x A.

exam.q: Explain why hydraulic systems use a liquid rather than a gas.
model: Liquids are (almost) incompressible
So pressure is transmitted equally throughout the liquid / the force is passed on
exam.tip: Incompressible is the key word.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of pressure, what causes upthrust on an object in water.
model: Pressure increases with depth
The bottom of the object is deeper than the top, so the pressure on the bottom is greater
This gives a larger upward force than downward force, a resultant upward force (upthrust)
exam.tip: Pressure difference leads to force difference.

exam.q: Explain why atmospheric pressure decreases with height above sea level.
model: Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of air above
At greater height there is less air above
The air is also less dense, so fewer particle collisions / less weight per unit area
exam.tip: Mention both less air above and lower density.

exam.q: A solid steel block sinks in water but a steel ship floats. Explain why.
model: An object floats when upthrust equals its weight
Upthrust equals the weight of water displaced
The steel block is denser than water so it cannot displace its own weight of water
It sinks because its weight is greater than the upthrust
The ship is hollow and contains air, so its average density is less than water
It displaces a large volume of water whose weight equals the ship's weight, so it floats
exam.tip: Compare the block and ship using density, weight and upthrust.

worked.q: A diver is at a depth of 25 m in sea water of density 1030 kg/m cubed. Atmospheric pressure is 100 000 Pa and g = 10 N/kg. Calculate the total pressure on the diver.
steps: Pressure due to water: p = h x rho x g = 25 x 1030 x 10
worked.ans: About 358 000 Pa (358 kPa), about 3.6 times atmospheric pressure.

worked.q: A car brake pedal pushes a master piston of area 2 cm squared with a force of 150 N. Each brake piston has an area of 12 cm squared. Find the force on each brake piston.
steps: Convert: 2 cm squared = 0.0002 m squared; 12 cm squared = 0.0012 m squared
Pressure is transmitted equally through the brake fluid
worked.ans: 900 N on each brake piston, six times the input force, because the area is six times larger.
